One Inc. v. Olesen. In January 1958, the Supreme Court issued a unanimous nine to zero decision affirming that a magazine published by a homophile organization could not be banned from the mail based solely on its LGBTQ content. The Court decided the case per curiam, issuing no signed opinion. The decision overturned the Post Office's attempt to exclude ONE Magazine, published by One Incorporated, from the mail on the grounds that it was obscene. The magazine contained a short story, poetry, and essays on homosexuality, but no explicit sexual content. The Post Office had objected to its very existence and subject matter. By affirming without commentary, the Supreme Court effectively barred the government from censoring materials simply because they discussed homosexuality openly. The Ninth Circuit's lower court decision had been momentous in itself, but the Supreme Court's affirmation gave it the weight of final authority. The ruling enabled the homophile movement to distribute its literature freely, contributing substantially to the growth of LGBTQ activism in the late nineteen fifties and nineteen sixties. One Inc. established an important First Amendment principle: the government cannot suppress speech based on viewpoint or subject matter alone. The case marked the first U.S. Supreme Court victory for LGBTQ rights and paved the way for the modern gay rights movement.
